# Each entry is a content fingerprint of one tolerated violation:
#   sha256(relpath | enclosing function | normalized matched line | nth-dup)
# Line numbers are NOT part of the key, so inserting lines above a tolerated
# violation does not re-report it. Editing that line, or moving/renaming the
# function around it, DOES — on purpose: the exemption was granted for
# specific code, so changed code deserves a fresh look.
#
# The text after `#` on an entry line is a pointer for humans. It is
# regenerated on every run and is never matched against.
#
# Reviewed in PR; remove entries as the code is cleaned up.
# ---- notes below this line are preserved across --update-baseline ----
#
# -- Why these three are here -------------------------------------------------
#
# All three match `.gitignore` line 27, `*api_key*` (lowercase, with the
# underscore). That glob exists to stop a file full of API keys being
# committed; it also matches the source of the API-key FEATURE, which is a
# different thing entirely.
#
# These files are tracked, so they work today. What they are not is safe: any
# one of them, deleted and recreated -- or added by a tool that does not force
# -- vanishes from the commit silently. Two are worth naming:
#
#   backend/app/routers/api_keys.py                    the API-key router itself
#   backend/migrations/versions/0056_api_key_...py     an Alembic migration; losing
#                                                      it breaks `upgrade head`
#                                                      for every deployment
#
# They are baselined rather than renamed on purpose. The names are correct --
# `api_keys.py` is exactly what that router should be called, and a migration
# filename is part of the revision chain. Renaming good code to appease an
# overbroad glob is backwards, and `git add -f` just moves the trap to whoever
# touches the file next.
#
# This list held EIGHT entries until five were pruned: the camelCase
# frontend/client sources (useApiKeys.ts, ApiKeysPage.tsx, apiKeyService.ts,
# apiKey.ts, ParallelSuitesWithOneApiKeyTest.java). Those spell the feature as
# `ApiKey` / `apiKey`, which does NOT contain the lowercase substring
# `api_key` or `apikey` and so never matched the globs on a case-sensitive
# filesystem -- git check-ignore is the authority, and on Linux CI it does not
# flag them. They were baselined (likely captured on a case-insensitive box)
# and had sat as permanent stale `!!` drift, training reviewers to tune out
# gate warnings. A test now pins this baseline at zero stale entries.
#
# The real fix for the three that DO match is to anchor the glob to the file
# types that actually carry secrets (`*api_key*.json`, `*.env`, `*.txt`, ...)
# so it stops matching source. That narrows a SECURITY control, so it is the
# owner's call, not this guard's -- see GIT-001 in docs/exploratory/BACKLOG.md.
# Clear these three by doing that, then re-run with --update-baseline.
